title: Detect Squares
description:
# Detect Squares

You are given a stream of points on the X-Y plane. Design an algorithm that supports two operations:

* `add(point)` inserts one point from the stream. Duplicate points are allowed, and each inserted copy is counted separately.
* `count(point)` returns how many ways there are to choose three previously added points so that those three points plus the query point form an axis-aligned square with positive area.

An axis-aligned square has four equal-length sides, and every side is parallel to either the x-axis or the y-axis. The query point is not inserted by `count`; it is only one corner of the square being counted.

Implement the `DetectSquares` class:

* `DetectSquares()` initializes an empty data structure.
* `void add(int[] point)` adds `point = [x, y]` to the data structure.
* `int count(int[] point)` counts all valid axis-aligned squares that use `point = [x, y]` as one corner.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1:

**Input**
["DetectSquares", "add", "add", "add", "count", "count", "add", "count"]
[[], [[3, 10]], [[11, 2]], [[3, 2]], [[11, 10]], [[14, 8]], [[11, 2]], [[11, 10]]]

**Output**
[null, null, null, null, 1, 0, null, 2]

**Explanation**
After adding `[3, 10]`, `[11, 2]`, and `[3, 2]`, the query `[11, 10]` completes one square.
The query `[14, 8]` completes no square.
Adding `[11, 2]` again creates a duplicate copy of one supporting corner, so the same query `[11, 10]` can now be counted in two ways.

## Constraints:

* `point.length == 2`
* `0 <= x, y <= 1000`
* At most `3000` total calls will be made to `add` and `count`.

solutions.name: Opposite Corner Hash Map
solutions.description:
## Approach
Store a count for every coordinate and also keep the full list of inserted points. During `count`, treat each inserted point as the possible opposite corner of the query square. If the horizontal and vertical distances are equal and non-zero, the other two corners are forced.

## Key Insight
Once the query corner and opposite corner are known, there is no freedom left: the missing corners must be `(queryX, oppositeY)` and `(oppositeX, queryY)`. Duplicate opposite corners are handled by iterating the inserted list, while duplicates of the other two corners multiply through their stored counts.

## Complexity Analysis
Time Complexity: O(P) per `count`, where P is the number of inserted points. Space Complexity: O(P) for the count map and insertion list.

solutions.name: Fixed Coordinate Grid
solutions.description:
## Approach
Use the coordinate bound `0 <= x, y <= 1000` directly. A `1001 x 1001` grid stores how many times each coordinate has appeared, while a list keeps every inserted point available for opposite-corner enumeration.

## Key Insight
The grid turns the two missing-corner lookups into direct array reads. This is a useful tradeoff when the coordinate range is small and fixed: memory increases, but lookup code becomes simpler and avoids hashing.

## Complexity Analysis
Time Complexity: O(P) per `count`. Space Complexity: O(C^2 + P), where C is the coordinate limit plus one.

solutions.name: Column Map Enumeration
solutions.description:
## Approach
Group counts by x-coordinate. For a query `(x, y)`, enumerate points already stored in the same column. Each different `otherY` defines a vertical side length, and the algorithm checks the two possible squares on the left and right.

## Key Insight
You do not need to scan every inserted point if you can enumerate only points that share the query column. The vertical side determines both horizontal directions, and duplicate points multiply by the count at the vertical endpoint and the two side corners.

## Complexity Analysis
Time Complexity: O(Kx) per `count`, where Kx is the number of distinct y-values in the query column. Space Complexity: O(U), where U is the number of distinct coordinates.

solutions.name: Row Map Enumeration
solutions.description:
## Approach
Store counts grouped by y-coordinate instead of x-coordinate. For a query `(x, y)`, enumerate points in the same row to define a horizontal side, then check the possible matching corners above and below that side.

## Key Insight
This is the row-symmetric form of column enumeration. Seeing both versions is useful because many design problems become faster when the data is indexed by the dimension that the query naturally fixes.

## Complexity Analysis
Time Complexity: O(Ky) per `count`, where Ky is the number of distinct x-values in the query row. Space Complexity: O(U), where U is the number of distinct coordinates.

solutions.name: Unique Opposite-Corner Enumeration
solutions.description:
## Approach
Keep counts for every coordinate, but enumerate only distinct coordinates as possible opposite corners. When a distinct opposite corner works, multiply by that coordinate's count and by the counts of the two remaining corners.

## Key Insight
The insertion-list approach counts duplicate opposite corners by visiting them repeatedly. This version counts the same multiplicity explicitly with `diagonalCount`, which can be much cheaper when the stream contains many repeated points.

## Complexity Analysis
Time Complexity: O(U) per `count`, where U is the number of distinct coordinates. Space Complexity: O(U) for the count map and unique-coordinate set.

tests.description: Canonical stream counts one square, then a duplicate supporting corner doubles the answer.
Four corners around the query form exactly one unit square.

tests.output: [null, null, null, null, null, null, null, null, null, 8]
tests.description: Duplicate copies of all three supporting corners multiply the count.
Counting before any points have been added returns zero.
Adding the query-corner point itself does not create extra squares.

tests.output: [null, null, null, null, null, null, null, 2]
tests.description: The same query can complete one square on the left and one square on the right.
Boundary coordinates at 0 and 1000 still form a valid square.
Duplicate opposite corners multiply the answer even when the side corners are unique.
A rectangle with unequal width and height must not be counted as a square.
